citingPaper.abstract: Global sensitivity analysis is essential for quantifying how tropical cyclone forecast uncertainties propagate through high-fidelity storm surge models, yet conventional methods face a fundamental trade-off between spatial resolution and computational tractability when outputs span hundreds of thousands of coastal mesh nodes. This paper presents a framework that integrates neural field surrogates into variance-based global sensitivity analysis of high-dimensional spatially distributed outputs. The proposed approach augments the surrogate input space with spatial coordinates, enabling a single neural network to learn a continuous mapping from storm parameters and geographic locations to local surge response. A positional encoding module mitigates the spectral bias of standard neural networks, preserving high-frequency sensitivity patterns near coastlines and storm tracks. Sobol indices are estimated through single-loop Monte Carlo integration over the trained surrogate. The framework is validated on an analytical benchmark with 62,500 output dimensions and then applied to a storm surge simulation of Superstorm Sandy across 100,000 unstructured mesh nodes, with four uncertain tropical cyclone track and intensity parameters as inputs. Results demonstrate that the proposed method reduces first-order and total-effect Sobol’ index estimation errors by 50%–75% compared to alternatives, replacing multiple dimensionality-reduction and surrogate-fitting steps with a single unified model. These improvements enable more reliable identification of the dominant drivers of storm surge risk uncertainty at fine spatial resolution.
